chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Murazim, from his father who said:

We went out with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when he left from the presence of Abu Ja'far Al-Mansur from Al-Hira. He left at the time permitted for him and arrived at Al-Saliheen at the beginning of the night. A tax collector, who was stationed at Al-Saliheen at the beginning of the night, presented himself to him and said, 'I will not let you pass.' So he urged him and requested him, but he refused firmly. I and Musaddaf were with him. Musaddaf said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you, this one is a dog; he has troubled you, and I fear he will make you return, and I do not know what will happen regarding the order of Abu Ja'far. If you permit us, I and Murazim can strike his neck and then throw him into the river?' He said, 'Restrain yourself, O Musaddaf.' He did not stop requesting him until most of the night had passed, so he permitted him. He passed. He said, 'O Murazim, is this better or that which you said?' I said, 'This is better, may I be sacrificed for you.' He said, 'Indeed, a man exits from minor humiliation, but that [action] causes him to enter into major humiliation.'

key_terms.أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ الْمَنْصُورُ: Abu Ja'far Al-Mansur, the Abbasid Caliph
key_terms.السَّالِحُونَ: Al-Saliheen, a district in Kufa known for tax collection

ai.seo_question: What is the lesson of humility and avoiding greater humiliation in the hadith of Imam Al-Sadiq and the tax collector?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights Imam Al-Sadiq’s strategic patience during his transit from the Abbasid capital, illustrating the Shia principle of *Taqiyya* (prudent dissimulation) and political prudence. By rejecting his companions' suggestion to kill the obstructing guard, he demonstrates that enduring minor, temporary humiliation prevents the greater, lasting humiliation of being perceived as a rebellious threat to the Caliphate. This narrative serves as a foundational example of how the Imams navigated the delicate balance between maintaining their spiritual authority and avoiding premature conflict with the ruling Umayyad and Abbasid powers.
